knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $\int 2 x^{2}\sqrt{x^{3} + 15}\,\text{d}x.$

Work on an interval where $x^{3} + 15>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $2 x^{2}$ outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(x^{3} + 15).$ But the derivative is $3 x^{2},$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u=x^{3} + 15.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3 x^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{2}{3}\,\text{d}u=2 x^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\int 2 x^{2}\sqrt{x^{3} + 15}\,\text{d}x=\frac{2}{3}\int u^{\frac{1}{2}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\int u^{\frac{1}{2}}\,\text{d}u &=\frac{2}{3}\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}+C\\ &=\frac{4}{9}u^{\frac{3}{2}}+C\\ &=\frac{4 \left(x^{3} + 15\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: real x; inner>0 for square roots

knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/problem:
Calculate $\int x\sqrt{x^{2} - 7}\,\text{d}x.$

Work on an interval where $x^{2} - 7>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $x$ outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(x^{2} - 7).$ But the derivative is $2 x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u=x^{2} - 7.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2 x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\int x\sqrt{x^{2} - 7}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int u^{\frac{1}{2}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int u^{\frac{1}{2}}\,\text{d}u &=\frac{1}{2}\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}+C\\ &=\frac{1}{3}u^{\frac{3}{2}}+C\\ &=\frac{\left(x^{2} - 7\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: real x; inner>0 for square roots
